findings.title: Profile-weight lookup is a per-agent Python loop, which breaks the slice's own defining rule
findings.description:
The weight array is built with `np.array([profiles[pi].cohesion_weight for pi in state.profile_indices[eval_indices]])`. That is a Python loop over every active agent, inside `BulkForce.__call__`, on every force call. It contradicts the slice's "defining constraint" (line 198: "No Python-level per-agent loops in any `BulkForce.__call__` implementation"). It also contradicts the architecture's rule against "Python-level per-agent branching" in the force hot loop (100-arch line 102). The grep check at lines 220-225 would not catch it, because it looks for `agent_idx`, `eval_indices` and `list_idx` loop variables only.

The fix is cheaper than the current design: loop over profiles, not agents, then gather. For example, `np.array([p.cohesion_weight for p in profiles])[state.profile_indices[eval_indices]]`. That costs O(n_profiles) Python steps and stays fully vectorized per agent. Replace the sketch and remove the line saying it "can be precomputed per tick if needed".

findings.title: Changing the BulkForce contract leaves slice 103's design out of date, with no plan to update it
findings.description:
The frontmatter lists `103-predator-prey-dynamics` as an interface (line 7). Line 178 says future forces such as predator-prey "consume this instead of raw lists." But 103's design (not started) is written entirely against the old contract:
- `FlightForce` and `PursuitForce` take `neighbor_lists`.
- Each force excludes the agent itself inline (`neighbors[neighbors != agent_idx]`).
- 103's success criteria say "Forces perform self-exclusion" and "one Python loop over active agents".
- 103 says "No changes to tick()" because forces receive `(state, neighbor_lists, profiles, active_indices)`.

Slice 109 makes all of that wrong:
- The signature changes (line 161).
- Self-exclusion moves into `build_neighbor_data` (line 194).
- Per-agent loops are banned.

Slice 109 should say what happens to 103. Either 103's design gets revised before it is implemented (signature, self-exclusion criterion, loop allowance), or 103 is explicitly allowed a per-agent loop for now. Without that, whichever slice lands second breaks the other's design.

findings.title: Padded layout memory is unbounded at the 10K-agent tier the architecture targets
findings.description:
The architecture's goal is "tens of thousands of agents at full behavioral fidelity on a single CPU process" (100-arch line 36). The slice sets `max_neighbors` to the maximum count across all agents (line 82), and its own premise is that clustering drives k toward n (line 17). The padded arrays are therefore O(n_active × n) when clustered. At n = 10K that is roughly:
- `indices`: about 800 MB
- `mask`: about 100 MB
- the `(n, k, 2)` float64 gather: about 1.6 GB, allocated again in every neighbor force

The claims that CSR offers "no benefit at n ≤ 10K" and that memory matters only at "100K+" are not supported by these numbers. One dense cluster also widens the padding for every agent.

This doesn't block the 100-agent fix, but the design should either:
- (a) state the agent-count and density range it is valid for, and record the limit against the architecture goal, or
- (b) adopt the lightweight fix now: process agent rows in fixed-size chunks inside the forces, which bounds peak memory and keeps the `NeighborData` interface.

Related overclaim: `max_neighbors` changes every tick, so the arrays are reallocated with a new shape every tick. The architecture's GPU path calls for "no dynamic allocation" (100-arch line 102), so lines 27 and 180 overstate how GPU-ready this layout is.

findings.title: The multi-tick old-vs-new integration test is too heavy and likely to fail spuriously
findings.description:
Line 260 calls for full `tick()` runs over N ticks, with positions and velocities matching between the old and new implementations. That means keeping the old `neighbor_lists` signature, the old forces and an old `tick()` path in the test suite, alongside the protocol this slice replaces.

Boid dynamics are sensitive to initial conditions. The vectorized masked `np.sum / count` adds floats in a different order from the old per-agent `np.mean`, and those tiny differences grow over many ticks. A multi-tick exact match is therefore unreliable even when both versions are correct.

The per-force equivalence tests (line 258) on identical inputs already show the two versions behave the same, and the existing `tick()` behavior tests cover the wiring. Cut the multi-tick old-vs-new test, or reduce it to a single tick.

findings.title: The `atol=1e-12` tolerance is not shown to hold for these force magnitudes
findings.description:
This finding concerns the single-call per-force equivalence tests, which remain the main correctness evidence once the multi-tick test is cut. Line 258 asserts `np.allclose(old_result, new_result, atol=1e-12)`. Line 190 only asks for agreement "within float64 tolerance".

`np.allclose` also has a default `rtol` of 1e-5, so a pure absolute check needs `rtol=0`. Absolute error is not uniform across these forces:
- Separation uses inverse-square terms that grow large at small distances.
- Cohesion averages positions that may be in the hundreds.

Different summation order (masked sum ÷ count vs `np.mean`) can produce differences close to, or above, 1e-12 for some inputs. The design should either show the absolute bound holds for the force magnitudes the tests use, or switch to a relative tolerance that fits the values involved.

findings.title: Padding with `-1` is still read; the mask only hides the result
findings.description: Line 80 says padded `-1` entries are "never dereferenced thanks to `mask`". In fact `state.positions[neighbor_data.indices]` does read them: NumPy treats `-1` as "last element", so every padded slot gathers agent n-1's data, and the masking step at line 114 overwrites it afterward. Any reduction that skips the mask will silently use agent n-1's data, for example the separation distance filter or the leadership-weighted mean. The text should say this, and the equivalence fixtures should place agent n-1 so that a missing mask changes the result.

findings.title: "Constant Python overhead" overstates the result; the 50 ms target is only in the walkthrough
findings.description: Line 19 claims "constant Python overhead, regardless of agent count." Steps 2 and 3 of the data flow (lines 95-96) are still O(n) Python loops (the per-agent query and the padding builder). The claim holds only for the forces themselves, which is what the slice plan says. The 50 ms / 100-agent target is stated at lines 23 and 215, but it is not listed under Success Criteria. Consider adding it there, measured with the server's existing overrun warning.

findings.title: MomentumForce is called "neighbor-dependent" but uses no neighbors
findings.description: Lines 35 and 190 group `MomentumForce` with the "five neighbor-dependent forces". Line 125 says it "does not use neighbors at all". Reword to "five per-agent-loop forces" or similar.

findings.title: Scope, layering and dependency direction match the plan and the architecture
findings.description:
- The slice covers everything its slice plan entry assigns: the padded representation, all five rewrites, and the protocol and caller changes in the same slice.
- It leaves spatial-query batching to slice 105 and keeps the `SpatialQuery` interface unchanged.
- It places `NeighborData` in `engine/neighbors.py`, so the spatial layer stays unaware of the padding, which matches the "Pluggable spatial queries" and "Clean boundaries" principles.
- Its stated value follows directly from the architecture's requirement that the hot loop be vectorized.
- There are no new I/O paths, so no I/O failure-mode list is needed.
- The edge cases it names (zero neighbors, single agent, active subset) cover the shapes that padding introduces.
